tagline: A herdsman from Judah walks into the prosperous northern kingdom of Israel and announces that God will judge a nation that worships loudly while crushing the poor.
overview:
Amos is usually counted the earliest of the prophets whose words were gathered into a book of their own, and it may be the most direct. Around the middle of the eighth century BC, a man from the village of Tekoa in Judah traveled north to the kingdom of Israel, which was enjoying its greatest wealth in generations under King Jeroboam II. The shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were crowded with worshipers, and the rich had built winter houses, summer houses, and homes decorated with ivory. Amos looked beneath the prosperity and saw courts that took bribes, creditors who sold debtors for the price of a pair of sandals, merchants who rigged their scales, and worship that God refused to accept.

The book opens with a series of judgments on Israel's neighbors for their war crimes, then springs its trap by turning the same judgment on Judah and, at greatest length, on Israel. Chapters 3 to 6 press the charges in sermons, laments, and woes. Chapters 7 to 9 record five visions of coming judgment and a clash with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, who tells Amos to go home. The book ends with a promise that God will raise up the fallen house of David and restore his people.

Amos matters because he refuses to separate the worship of God from the treatment of neighbors. His line "let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24) has been quoted for centuries by people who wanted faith to show itself in public life. He also teaches that privilege before God brings accountability rather than immunity, and that the Day of the LORD is not good news for those who assume they are safe.
author:
The book presents itself as "the words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa" (Amos 1:1). In 7:14-15 Amos says he was not a professional prophet or a member of a prophetic guild but a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees whom the LORD took from following the flock. The word used for sheepherder in 1:1 is used elsewhere of King Mesha of Moab, who paid tribute in sheep (2 Kings 3:4), so some scholars think Amos was a substantial owner or manager of flocks rather than a poor hired hand; others think he was a working shepherd. Either way he was a layman from Judah speaking in the north.

Most scholars accept that the core of the book comes from Amos himself, whose oracles were collected and arranged by him or by those who preserved his words. Many critical scholars regard certain passages as later additions: the oracle against Judah (2:4-5), the hymn-like doxologies praising God as creator (4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6), and the closing promise of restoration (9:11-15). Other scholars argue that each of these fits Amos's own setting and that the hopeful ending is the natural completion of a message of judgment. The book as it stands has been read as a unity by Jewish and Christian readers throughout their history.
date:
The superscription dates Amos's preaching to the reigns of Uzziah king of Judah (about 792 to 740 BC) and Jeroboam II king of Israel (about 793 to 753 BC), and more precisely to "two years before the earthquake" (1:1). Exact dates for these kings vary by a few years among scholars because of overlapping co-regencies. Most place Amos's ministry around 760 BC, and it may have been brief, perhaps a single season or a single year.

The earthquake was remembered long afterward; Zechariah 14:5 still refers to people fleeing "from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah". Excavators at Hazor in the north of Israel, and at several other sites in the region, have reported damage layers from a strong earthquake that they date to roughly the middle of the eighth century BC. Linking these directly to the earthquake of Amos 1:1 is reasonable and widely suggested, but archaeological dating is approximate, and the connection remains probable rather than certain. The book was likely written down not long after Amos's preaching, with debate, as noted above, about whether some passages were added later.
setting:
The first half of the eighth century was a season of unusual peace and expansion for Israel and Judah. Assyria, the great power of Mesopotamia, was for several decades preoccupied with internal troubles and other enemies, and Aram (Syria), Israel's northern rival, had been weakened. Jeroboam II took advantage of this and extended Israel's borders to the north and east (2 Kings 14:25), while Uzziah did the same for Judah. Trade flourished, and a class of wealthy landowners and officials grew in Samaria, the capital. Excavations at Samaria recovered carved ivory inlays from this general period, and inscribed potsherds (the Samaria ostraca) recording deliveries of wine and oil to the capital, which help modern readers picture the world Amos describes.

The prosperity was unevenly shared. Small farmers could fall into debt after a bad harvest, lose their land, and be sold into servitude; courts that met in the city gate could be bought. Worship flourished at royal shrines such as Bethel, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf generations earlier, and at Gilgal and Beersheba. Within a few years of Jeroboam II's death, Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III (who came to the throne in 745 BC) returned to the west, and in 722 BC Samaria fell and the northern kingdom came to an end. Amos's warnings came about a generation before that collapse.
purpose: Amos was sent to announce to Israel that its end was near and to explain why. The reasons were concrete: oppression of the poor and weak, corruption in the courts, sexual abuse, luxurious living funded by injustice, and a religion that multiplied sacrifices and songs while ignoring what God had commanded. He also called the people to "Seek the LORD and live" (Amos 5:6), leaving open the possibility that God might be gracious to a remnant. The book was preserved so that Judah, and every later community of God's people, could learn from Israel's fall and recognize that God's covenant love includes his demand for justice.
story: Amos stands at the beginning of the great era of the writing prophets, just before Hosea in the north and Isaiah and Micah in the south. The story behind him is the history told in 1 and 2 Kings: the division of Solomon's kingdom, the northern kings' rival shrines at Bethel and Dan, and centuries of prophetic warnings from figures such as Elijah and Elisha. Amos appeals constantly to the exodus, the wilderness years, and the gift of the land, and his social charges echo the laws of the covenant about debt, pledges, fair weights, and justice in court. After him, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC confirmed his words, and his closing promise of a restored house of David points forward to the hope carried by the later prophets and fulfilled, in the New Testament's reading, in Jesus.
christ: Amos's final chapter promises that God will "restore the fallen tent of David" (Amos 9:11). At the Jerusalem council in Acts 15, James quoted this passage, following the wording of the Greek translation of the Old Testament, to show that the inclusion of Gentiles in the church fulfilled what the prophets had said: the risen Christ, David's heir, was rebuilding David's house so that the nations might seek the Lord. Stephen also quoted Amos 5:25-27 in his speech in Acts 7 to show Israel's long history of idolatry. More broadly, Amos's demand that worship and justice belong together is taken up in Jesus's own teaching, as when he rebuked those who tithed garden herbs but neglected justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23). These links are partly direct fulfillment and partly shared conviction, and it is worth keeping the two distinct.
reading: Amos is poetry and prophetic speech, with one short narrative (7:10-17) and a series of visions. Watch for the repeated formula that opens each oracle in chapters 1 and 2, beginning with "For three transgressions of Damascus, even four", the call to "Hear this word" that opens chapters 3, 4, and 5, the refrain "yet you did not return to Me" in chapter 4, and the woes of chapters 5 and 6. Amos uses shocking images (cows of Bashan, a lion's roar, a basket of summer fruit that sounds like the word for the end), and his rhetoric is meant to jolt. Read his social charges for what they name: specific acts of oppression and corruption measured against Israel's covenant law. Readers across the political spectrum have claimed him, but the text itself addresses God's people and their leaders, and its standard is God's covenant, not any modern program. Do not skip the ending; the book closes on restoration.

structure.title: Judgment on the nations, then on Judah and Israel
structure.summary: Eight oracles in the same pattern condemn Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, and finally Israel, whose oppression of the poor receives the longest indictment.

structure.title: Hear this word: privilege and accountability
structure.summary: Because God chose Israel, he will hold it to account. The wealthy of Samaria, the shrines of Bethel, and a people who refused every earlier warning are summoned to meet their God.

structure.title: Lament and woe
structure.summary: A funeral song for fallen Israel, a call to seek the LORD and establish justice, a warning that the Day of the LORD will be darkness, and woes on the complacent rich.

structure.title: Five visions and a confrontation
structure.summary: Visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line, summer fruit, and the Lord at the altar announce judgment, interrupted by Amaziah the priest's order that Amos leave Bethel.

structure.title: The fallen tent of David restored
structure.summary: After judgment, God will raise up the house of David, restore his people's fortunes, and plant them in their land never again to be uprooted.

themes.title: Justice and righteousness
themes.body: Amos pairs two words that run through the whole Old Testament: justice (mishpat), the right ordering of life and especially fair judgment in court, and righteousness (tsedaqah), faithfulness to the obligations of the covenant community. Amos condemns selling the needy, taking bribes, turning away the poor at the gate, and cheating with false weights. For him these are not side issues but the measure of whether a people truly knows God.

themes.title: Worship without obedience
themes.body: Israel's shrines were busy and its offerings generous, but God says he hates their feasts and will not listen to their songs (Amos 5:21-23). Amos does not reject worship as such; he rejects worship that is used as a cover for injustice or as a substitute for obedience. The prophets who followed him, and Jesus after them, made the same point.

themes.title: Election and accountability
themes.body: "Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (Amos 3:2). Israel assumed that being God's chosen people guaranteed its safety. Amos turns the logic around: those who have received more knowledge of God and more of his gifts will answer for more.

themes.title: God of all nations and all creation
themes.body: Amos's God judges Damascus and Moab for crimes against humanity, brought the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir (9:7), forms the mountains, and names the stars. He is not a tribal deity bound to one land. That universal rule is the ground both for his judgment of Israel and for the hope of a restoration in which the nations bear his name (9:12).

themes.title: The Day of the LORD
themes.body: Israel looked forward to the Day of the LORD as a day of victory over its enemies. Amos, in one of the earliest uses of the phrase in the prophets, warns that it will be darkness and not light for a disobedient people (Amos 5:18-20). The theme recurs throughout the later prophets and into the New Testament.

keyChapters.why: The superscription sets Amos in time and place, and the oracles against the nations show a God who holds every people accountable for cruelty.
The trap closes: after condemning the neighbors, Amos turns on Israel and names its oppression of the poor in concrete detail.
The principle of election and accountability, and the chain of questions that explains why a prophet must speak.
The book's heart: a lament over Israel, the call to seek the LORD and live, the warning about the Day of the LORD, and the demand that justice roll like a river.
Amos's visions and his confrontation with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, show the prophet's calling and the cost of speaking.
The final vision of judgment gives way to the promise of David's restored tent, quoted by James at the Jerusalem council.
